GEO-9#6.text: Work from the top of the tree instead. From that corner the opposite side is the ground, 40 ft, and the adjacent side is the tree, 50 ft. So the tangent there is 40 ÷ 50 = 0.8, and the angle is tan⁻¹(0.8) ≈ 38.7°. The two acute angles of a right triangle add to 90°, so the angle of elevation is 90 − 38.7 = 51.3°.

GEO-9#7.title: Find the other leg first
GEO-9#7.text: Find the leg across from the 55° angle: 20 × sin 55° ≈ 20 × 0.8192 ≈ 16.38. Then use the Pythagorean theorem for x: x² = 20² − 16.38² ≈ 400 − 268.3 = 131.7, so x ≈ 11.5. It agrees with the cosine answer, and it uses only the sine key and the three sides.

GEO-9#8.title: Use the angle at the clifftop
GEO-9#8.text: Inside the triangle, the angle at the top of the cliff is between the cliff face and the line of sight. It is 90 − 25 = 65°. From that corner the distance to the boat is the opposite side and the 60 m cliff is the adjacent side. So tan 65° = d ÷ 60, and d = 60 × tan 65° ≈ 60 × 2.1445 ≈ 129 m. Multiplying replaces the division.

GEO-9#9.title: Find the rise first
GEO-9#9.text: First find how high the ramp climbs: rise = 10 × sin 12° ≈ 10 × 0.2079 ≈ 2.08 m. Then use the Pythagorean theorem for the ground distance: x² = 10² − 2.08² ≈ 100 − 4.32 = 95.68, so x ≈ 9.78 m. The ground distance is only a little shorter than the ramp because the angle is small.

GEO-10#1.title: Cut from a point inside
GEO-10#1.text: Pick a point in the middle of a hexagon and join it to all 6 corners. That makes 6 triangles, worth 6 × 180 = 1080°. But the angles packed around the middle point are not corners of the hexagon. They make a full turn, 360°, so take them away: 1080 − 360 = 720°. For n sides this is n × 180 − 360, which is the same as (n − 2) × 180.

GEO-10#2.title: Check three regular shapes
GEO-10#2.text: Try it with numbers. An equilateral triangle has interior angles of 60°, so each exterior angle is 120°, and 3 × 120 = 360. A square has exterior angles of 90°, and 4 × 90 = 360. A regular hexagon has interior angles of 120°, so each exterior angle is 60°, and 6 × 60 = 360. More sides mean smaller turns, but the total never changes.

GEO-10#3.title: Like dogs and poodles
GEO-10#3.text: Every poodle is a dog, but not every dog is a poodle. In the same way, every square is a rectangle and every square is a rhombus, but most rectangles and rhombuses are not squares. Test a shape with a checklist. A 3 by 5 rectangle has two pairs of parallel sides and four right angles, but its sides are not all equal. So it is a parallelogram and a rectangle, and it is not a rhombus or a square.

GEO-10#4.title: Cut from the centre
GEO-10#4.text: Join the centre of the octagon to all 8 corners. This makes 8 triangles, worth 8 × 180 = 1440°. The 8 angles that meet at the centre are not corners of the octagon, and together they make a full turn of 360°. Remove them: 1440 − 360 = 1080°.

GEO-10#5.title: Six equilateral triangles
GEO-10#5.text: Join the centre of a regular hexagon to its 6 corners. The 6 angles at the centre are 360 ÷ 6 = 60° each, and the two sides from the centre are equal, so every triangle is equilateral with three 60° angles. At each corner of the hexagon two of these triangles meet. The interior angle is 60 + 60 = 120°.

GEO-10#6.title: Count triangles from one corner
GEO-10#6.text: Draw diagonals from one corner of the hexagon to the three corners that are not next to it. The hexagon splits into 4 triangles, so its angles total 4 × 180 = 720°. The hexagon is regular, so the 6 angles are equal, and each is 720 ÷ 6 = 120°. This matches 180 − 60 from the exterior angle.

GEO-10#7.title: Check with the interior angles
GEO-10#7.text: Test the answer 15 from the inside. A 15-sided polygon cuts into 15 − 2 = 13 triangles, so its angles total 13 × 180 = 2340°. Each interior angle of the regular one is 2340 ÷ 15 = 156°. The exterior angle beside it is 180 − 156 = 24°, which matches the given angle. So the polygon has 15 sides.

GEO-10#8.title: Use the total of 360
GEO-10#8.text: The four angles of any quadrilateral total 360°. In a parallelogram opposite angles are equal, so angles A and C are both 65° and use 130°. That leaves 360 − 130 = 230° for angles B and D, which are also equal. Each is 230 ÷ 2 = 115°. The angles are 65°, 115°, 65°, 115°.

GEO-10#9.title: Walk around the sign
GEO-10#9.text: Walk along the edge of the stop sign. At each of the 8 corners you turn by the same amount, and after all 8 you have made one full turn. Each turn is 360 ÷ 8 = 45°. The turn and the inside corner lie along a straight line, so the interior angle is 180 − 45 = 135°.

GEO-11#1.title: A stage seen from two seats
GEO-11#1.text: Picture a round arena with a stage along part of the wall, covering an 80° arc. From the exact centre, the stage fills 80° of your view. Now sit at the wall on the far side. You are further from the stage, and it fills only 40° of your view. Move to any other seat on that far wall and it still fills 40°. Centre seats see the arc itself, and wall seats see half of it.

GEO-11#2.title: A wheel on a flat road
GEO-11#2.text: Think of a wheel resting on a flat road. The road is a tangent, because it touches the wheel at one point. The axle sits directly above that point, so the spoke from the axle to the road points straight down while the road runs level. Straight down and level meet at 90°. If the spoke leaned, the axle would be lower than one radius above the road and the wheel would sink into it.

GEO-11#3.title: One slice of a pizza
GEO-11#3.text: Take a pizza with radius 10 inches. Its crust is 2 × π × 10 = 20π inches long and its area is π × 10² = 100π square inches. Cut a 36° slice. Since 36 ÷ 360 = 1/10, the slice is one tenth of the pizza. It gets one tenth of the crust, 2π inches, and one tenth of the area, 10π square inches. The same fraction works for both.

GEO-11#4.title: Go through the centre
GEO-11#4.text: Draw the inscribed angle so one of its sides passes through the centre. Join the centre to the other end of the arc. The central angle on the 110° arc is 110°. The two radii make an isosceles triangle, and the 110° angle is an exterior angle of it, so it equals the two equal base angles together. Each base angle is 110 ÷ 2 = 55°, and one of them is the inscribed angle.

GEO-11#5.title: Two isosceles triangles
GEO-11#5.text: Join the centre to the vertex of the angle. Now there are three equal radii, to the vertex and to each end of the diameter, and they form two isosceles triangles. Call their base angles a and b. The big triangle has angles a, b and a + b at the vertex, so 2a + 2b = 180°. That makes a + b = 90°, and a + b is the inscribed angle.

GEO-11#6.title: Spot the 5, 12, 13 triangle
GEO-11#6.text: The radius meets the tangent at 90°, so the line to the centre, 13, is the hypotenuse and the radius, 5, is a leg. A hypotenuse of 13 with a leg of 5 is the whole-number right triangle 5, 12, 13. The tangent is the other leg, so t = 12. Quick check without squaring 13: (13 − 5)(13 + 5) = 8 × 18 = 144 = 12².

GEO-11#7.title: Take a fraction of the circumference
GEO-11#7.text: Stay in degrees. The angle 60° is 60 ÷ 360 = 1/6 of a full turn. The whole circumference is 2 × π × 9 = 18π. One sixth of that is 18π ÷ 6 = 3π. The fraction method and the radian method agree: s = 3π.

GEO-11#8.title: Treat the slice like a triangle
GEO-11#8.text: A thin slice is nearly a triangle whose base is the crust and whose height is the radius. The whole crust is 2 × π × 6 = 12π, so one of 8 slices has 12π ÷ 8 = 1.5π inches of crust. Area = ½ × crust × radius = ½ × 1.5π × 6 = 4.5π, about 14.1 square inches.

GEO-11#9.title: Why equal, then test x
GEO-11#9.text: Join the centre O to P, A and B. Triangles OAP and OBP both have a right angle where the radius meets the tangent, they share the side OP, and OA = OB because both are radii. They are congruent by HL, so PA = PB. Now test x = 5 in the expression: 3 × 5 + 2 = 17, which matches the other tangent. So x = 5.

GEO-12#1.title: Count squares on a grid
GEO-12#1.text: Draw the shapes on grid paper. A rectangle 6 wide and 4 tall holds 24 squares. Lean it over into a parallelogram with base 6 and height 4 and it still holds 24. Cut that along a diagonal and each triangle has 12. A trapezoid with bases 4 and 8 and height 4 holds as much as a rectangle 6 wide, 24 again. A circle of radius 2 covers a little over 3 squares of side 2, about 12.6.

GEO-12#2.title: Push a deck of cards
GEO-12#2.text: Stack a deck of cards neatly and look at it from the side. You see a rectangle. Push the top sideways so the deck leans. The side view is now a parallelogram with a longer slanted edge, but no card was added or removed, so the area of the side view is the same. The deck is still the same number of cards tall. That straight-up thickness is the height, and the slanted edge is not.

GEO-12#3.title: A picture frame both ways
GEO-12#3.text: A frame is 10 by 8 on the outside with a 6 by 4 opening, and the border is 2 wide all round. Subtract: 80 − 24 = 56. Or add the pieces: the top and bottom strips are 10 by 2, which is 20 each, and the two side strips are 2 by 4, which is 8 each. That gives 20 + 20 + 8 + 8 = 56. Both plans agree, so choose the shorter one.

GEO-12#4.title: Rectangle plus two triangles
GEO-12#4.text: Drop two heights from the ends of the short base. The middle is a rectangle 8 wide and 5 tall, with area 40. The two triangles at the sides share the extra base length, 14 − 8 = 6, and both have height 5. Pushed together they make one triangle with area ½ × 6 × 5 = 15. The total is 40 + 15 = 55.

GEO-12#5.title: Unroll the ring
GEO-12#5.text: Cut the ring and straighten it into a strip. The strip is 5 − 3 = 2 wide. Its length is the circumference of the circle halfway through the ring, with radius 4, which is 2 × π × 4 = 8π. Area = length × width = 8π × 2 = 16π, about 50.3.

GEO-12#6.title: Count 6 by 4 blocks
GEO-12#6.text: The missing corner is 6 by 4, and the full 12 by 8 rectangle is exactly two of those blocks wide and two blocks tall. So the rectangle holds 4 blocks, and the L-shape is 3 of them. Each block has area 6 × 4 = 24, so the L-shape has area 3 × 24 = 72 square units.

GEO-12#7.title: Sort edges by direction
GEO-12#7.text: Group the edges instead of walking around. The horizontal edges are the 12 at the bottom and the two pieces of 6 above it, and 6 + 6 also makes 12. So the horizontal edges total 24. The vertical edges are the 8 on one side and the two pieces of 4 on the other, so they total 16. P = 24 + 16 = 40 units.

GEO-12#8.title: Box in the half circle
GEO-12#8.text: The half circle fits inside a 4 by 2 box with area 8. A circle fills about 78.5% of the square around it, and half a circle fills the same share of half the square. So the half circle is about 0.785 × 8 ≈ 6.28 square feet. Add the 4 by 3 rectangle: 12 + 6.28 ≈ 18.3 square feet. The answer sits between 12 and 20, as it should.

GEO-12#9.title: Cut and slide a triangle
GEO-12#9.text: Cut a right triangle off one end of the parallelogram with a straight up-and-down cut, and slide it to the other end. The shape becomes a rectangle with the same base, 10, and a side equal to the height, 5. Its area is 10 × 5 = 50. The slanted side 6 does not appear in the rectangle at all, which is why it is not used.

GEO-13#1.title: Check with real numbers
GEO-13#1.text: A box 4 by 3 by 5 has 12 unit cubes on its bottom layer and 5 layers, so 60 cubes. A cylinder with radius 3 and height 4 holds 9π × 4 = 36π, and the cone inside it holds a third, 12π. A sphere of radius 3 just fits in a cylinder of radius 3 and height 6, which holds 54π. The sphere fills two thirds of it: 36π, the same as (4/3) × π × 27.

GEO-13#2.title: Wrap a cereal box
GEO-13#2.text: Think of covering a 4 by 3 by 5 box with paper, one face at a time. Top and bottom are 4 by 3, so 12 each. Front and back are 4 by 5, so 20 each. The two ends are 3 by 5, so 15 each. The paper needed is 12 + 12 + 20 + 20 + 15 + 15 = 94 square units. For a can, the label peels off as a rectangle, and the two lids are circles.

GEO-13#3.title: Double a small box
GEO-13#3.text: A 2 by 3 by 4 box has surface area 2 × (6 + 8 + 12) = 52 and volume 24. Double every edge to get 4 by 6 by 8. The surface area is 2 × (24 + 32 + 48) = 208, which is 4 times 52. The volume is 4 × 6 × 8 = 192, which is 8 times 24. One doubling gives 2² = 4 for area and 2³ = 8 for volume.

GEO-13#4.title: Compare with a square box
GEO-13#4.text: Put the cylinder inside a box 6 by 6 by 10, which holds 360. Looking down, the circle fills π/4 of the 6 by 6 square, because 9π ÷ 36 = π/4. Every layer has that same share, so the cylinder holds 360 × π/4 = 90π, about 282.7. That is a bit over three quarters of the box, which looks right.

GEO-13#5.title: Use the cone formula directly
GEO-13#5.text: Use V = (1/3) × π × r² × h in one line. Here r² = 9 and h = 4. Divide by 3 early to keep numbers small: 9 ÷ 3 = 3, and 3 × 4 = 12. So V = 12π, about 37.7. Dividing the 9 first avoids building the 36π cylinder at all.

GEO-13#6.title: Two thirds of its cylinder
GEO-13#6.text: A sphere of radius 3 just fits inside a cylinder with radius 3 and height 6. That cylinder holds π × 9 × 6 = 54π. A sphere always fills two thirds of the cylinder that wraps it, so V = (2/3) × 54π = 36π, about 113.1. This matches the formula.

GEO-13#7.title: A band plus two lids
GEO-13#7.text: Stand the box on its 4 by 3 base. The four upright faces unfold into one long band. Its length is the distance around the base, 4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 14, and its width is the height, 5, so the band has area 70. The top and bottom are 12 each, which adds 24. SA = 70 + 24 = 94 square units.

GEO-13#8.title: Change to decimetres first
GEO-13#8.text: One litre is a cube 10 cm on each side, which is 1 decimetre each way. Change the tank to decimetres: 50 cm = 5 dm, 30 cm = 3 dm, 40 cm = 4 dm. Then V = 5 × 3 × 4 = 60 cubic decimetres, which is 60 L straight away. Each litre is 1000 cm³, so that is 60,000 cm³.

GEO-13#9.title: Stack copies of the small box
GEO-13#9.text: Fill the big box with copies of the small one. Three fit along each edge, so it takes 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 small boxes. The volume is 27 × 60 = 1620. Each face of the big box is tiled by 3 × 3 = 9 copies of the matching small face, so the surface area is 9 × 94 = 846. SA grows by 9 and V grows by 27.

GEO-14#1.title: Follow one point
GEO-14#1.text: Plot the point (3, 1) and apply each move to it. Reflect over the x-axis and it drops to (3, −1). Reflect over the y-axis and it jumps to (−3, 1). Rotate it a quarter turn counterclockwise about the origin and it lands on (−1, 3). Dilate it by 2 and it moves out to (6, 2). Watching one point shows which coordinate changes sign, which ones swap, and which ones grow.

GEO-14#2.title: Measure before and after
GEO-14#2.text: Take the triangle (0, 0), (3, 0), (0, 4). Its sides are 3, 4 and 5. Slide it 2 to the right: (2, 0), (5, 0), (2, 4). The sides are still 3, 4 and 5. Reflect it over the x-axis and they are still 3, 4 and 5. Now dilate by 2: (0, 0), (6, 0), (0, 8). The sides are 6, 8 and 10. The right angle is still there, but every length has doubled.

GEO-14#3.title: One segment, three questions
GEO-14#3.text: Join A(0, 0) to B(4, 2). It rises 2 while running 4, so its slope is 1/2. Turn the step "4 right, 2 up" a quarter turn and it becomes "2 left, 4 up", a slope of −2. That is the perpendicular slope, and 1/2 × −2 = −1. The midpoint is halfway in each direction, (2, 1). The length is √(4² + 2²) = √20, about 4.47.

GEO-14#4.title: Fold along the axis
GEO-14#4.text: Plot (3, −2) and fold the paper along the x-axis. The point is 2 units below the fold, so it lands 2 units above the fold, straight up from where it was. Count it: from (3, −2) go up 2 to reach the axis at (3, 0), then up 2 more. The image is (3, 2). The point never moved left or right, so x stayed 3.

GEO-14#5.title: Check with slope and distance
GEO-14#5.text: Test the answer (−5, 2). The line from the origin to (2, 5) has slope 5/2. The line to (−5, 2) has slope 2 ÷ (−5) = −2/5. Their product is −1, so the two lines are perpendicular, a 90° turn. Both points are √(4 + 25) = √29 from the origin. And (−5, 2) is to the left, which is where a counterclockwise turn sends a point from Quadrant I.

GEO-14#6.title: Repeat each walk
GEO-14#6.text: Reach each corner by a walk from the origin, then do the same walk again. To (1, 1): 1 right, 1 up; again gives (2, 2). To (3, 1): 3 right, 1 up; again gives (6, 2). To (1, 2): 1 right, 2 up; again gives (2, 4). Each image is twice as far out in the same direction, so the image is (2, 2), (6, 2), (2, 4).

GEO-14#7.title: Use two reflections
GEO-14#7.text: A quarter turn counterclockwise can be done with two mirror flips. First reflect (2, 5) over the diagonal line y = x, which swaps the coordinates: (5, 2). Then reflect over the y-axis, which changes the sign of x: (−5, 2). Two reflections across mirrors 45° apart make a 90° turn, so the image is (−5, 2).

GEO-14#8.title: Check the diagonals
GEO-14#8.text: A quadrilateral is a parallelogram when its diagonals cut each other in half. One diagonal joins (0, 0) and (5, 4). Its midpoint is (2.5, 2). The other joins (4, 1) and (1, 3). Its midpoint is ((4 + 1) ÷ 2, (1 + 3) ÷ 2) = (2.5, 2). Both diagonals have the same midpoint, so they bisect each other and the quadrilateral is a parallelogram.

GEO-14#9.title: Step straight across the mirror
GEO-14#9.text: The shortest way to the line y = x is at right angles to it, which means stepping 1 right and 1 down each time. From (1, 4), one step gives (2, 3), and half a step more gives (2.5, 2.5), which is on the mirror. That was 1.5 steps. Take 1.5 more steps the same way: (2.5 + 1.5, 2.5 − 1.5) = (4, 1). The image is (4, 1).
